newsitem.title: USA: Hasidic community members indicted for fraud.
newsitem.headline: Hasidic community members indicted for fraud.

text.p: Six men affiliated with a Hasidic Jewish community, the Village of New Square, were indicted on Wednesday for scheming to obtain tens of millions of dollars through federal and state grant, loan and subsidy programmes.

The indictment filed in Manhattan federal court alleged the men participated in the fraudulent schemes to benefit themselves and other residents of New Square, which is located in Rockland County northwest of New York City.

In December 1995 a federal judge appointed a receiver to control the Yeshiva of New Square in the first federal takeover of a Jewish religious school following repeated refusals by the institution to turn over financial records in a fraud investigation.
In the case announced by prosecutors on Wednesday, the defendants were charged with creating entities through which federal and state funds could be obtained.

They were also accused of submitting false documents to establish the eligibility of New Square residents to participate in the programmes, using the funds obtained from the programmes for impermissible purposes and hiding their fraud by using fake names and nominee bank accounts.

Among the programmes defrauded were the Pell Grant programme funded by the U.S. Department of Education, the Tuition Assistance Programme (TAP) funded by the New York State Department of Education and the U.S. Department of Education and a Small Business Administration programme designed to provide venture capital to small, minority-owned businesses.
The Pell Grant programme provides funds to financially needy post-secondary students who seek to obtain degrees or vocational certificates.

The defendants allegedly used fraudulent means to conceal that many of these "students" were ineligible to receive financial aid because they were not seeking degrees or because they were still in high school.
The indictment said the seminary fraudulently obtained $10.3 million in Pell Grants on behalf of its purported students.

All of the defendants were affiliated with the seminary according to the indictment. Among them was Chaim Berger, 71, who was chairman of the seminary's board, and Avrum Friesel, 44, who was the financial aid officer.
